During climb, VNAV honors climb altitude constraints, holding specified altitudes until the constraint is cleared or the waypoint is reached. Conditions triggering transitions to different climb modes include: nearing a constraint altitude, where VNAV sequences to VALTS, VALTV, or VALT; or when the preselect altitude is raised while at a constraint, leading to VNAV sequencing to VFLC to resume climb. Messages like "UNABLE NEXT ALT" or "CHECK FPLN ALT" alert the crew to potential violations or incorrect selections.
Target Speed, Transition Altitude, and Speed/Altitude Limit.

In a flight plan, waypoints can display climb or descent applicability (↑ for climb, ↓ for descent), an altitude constraint, a vertical path angle, and a speed constraint. An amber altitude constraint signifies that the current rate of climb or descent is insufficient to meet the specified flight plan altitude constraints, or that climb/descent altitude constraints are out of order, or that a climb altitude constraint is lower than a preceding one, or that a descent altitude constraint is higher than a preceding one, or that an altitude constraint is higher than the defined Cruise Altitude.

The current rate of climb or descent is not sufficient to meet the specified flight plan altitude constraints; All climb altitude constraints do not occur before all descent altitude constraints (except for the missed approach procedure); A climb altitude constraint is lower than the climb altitude constraint that comes before it; A descent altitude constraint is higher than the descent altitude constraint that comes before it; An altitude constraint is higher than the Cruise Altitude (CRZ ALT) that was defined on the PERF INIT page.

During the cruise phase, the FMS position can be updated through runway update, GNSS position, and position data obtained from navigation facilities or the FMS itself. Specifically, the FMS position can be updated from a GNSS sensor or from a selected Navigation Aid (NAVAID) en route, utilizing the UPDATE FROM NAVAID feature when the GNSS sensor is not available.
On the ground, the FMS position can be updated through runway position, an AIRPORT entry, a PILOT/REF WPT entry, or a GATE entry.

RWY UPDATE updates the FMS position to the runway threshold coordinates, which increases the navigational accuracy of the FMS when the GNSS sensor is disabled.

The FMS position can be updated en route using a Navigation Aid (NAVAID) by following these steps: push the INDEX function key, push the POS INIT LSK, push the NEXT function key to display the POS INIT 2/2 page, if necessary, enter the NAVAID identifier into the scratchpad and transfer it to the NAVAID data line (R5), push the UPDATE FROM NAVAID LSK, and finally push the CONFIRM POS LSK to update the position. This function is available only when the aircraft is airborne and when the GNSS sensor is not available.

During the climb phase, VNAV CLIMB allows the aircraft to climb to each constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. If the preselect altitude is raised while at a constraint altitude and an altitude change mode (FLC, VS, or PTCH) is selected, VNAV allows the aircraft to leave the constraint altitude, but may display "CHECK FPLN ALT" or "CHECK PRESELECTOR" messages if certain conditions are not met. When approaching a constraint, VNAV sequences to VALTS or VALTV. If the preselect altitude is not raised sufficiently before reaching the constraint, aural alerts and messages are issued, and VNAV may sequence to VFLC to resume climb after crossing the waypoint.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode is activated during Altitude Capture, either when a new attitude is selected or when maintaining the current altitude. The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode automatically activates when the aircraft's Mach number exceeds Mmo + 0.01 or airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. The AT system is only approved for Category I precision approach operations for Overspeed and Underspeed Protection.
OSPD Mode can be deselected by manually selecting another vertical mode when airspeed is below Vmo + 5 kt or Mmo + 0.01, or it will cancel automatically if airspeed decreases to Vmo/Mmo.

The parallel offset function ensures that the aircraft is horizontally parallel offset according to the offset distance set by the crew along the original flight plan. While tracking an offset path, course heading and deviation are referenced to the offset path. Responses: The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft using information from the FMS, radio navigation aids, or pilot input. It consists of two Flight Generators (FGs), two Flight Directors (FDs), one Autopilot (AP), one Autothrottle (AT), three Yaw Dampers (YDs), and one Mach Trim system. The system controls aircraft pitch, roll, and thrust via the pitch servo, roll servo, and AT servo.

In the PTCH Mode, the FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at Mode selection.

The ALTS Mode is activated during Altitude Capture when a new attitude is selected or when maintaining the current altitude. It is always armed, except when ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. The ALTS Mode is armed if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft when the vertical mode is GA. Rotating the ALT knob on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) will inhibit the ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes.

The Vertical Speed (VS) Mode is selected by pressing the VS Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) and commands the Autoflight System to maintain a preselected vertical speed. It can be deselected by pressing the VS Button again, changing the mode to PTCH, or by selecting other vertical modes.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.

The OSPD Mode is automatically activated to prevent the aircraft speed from exceeding Vmo/Mmo by generating pitch commands to reduce the airspeed.
The USPD Mode is activated to prevent stall stick shaker by generating pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman.

Discontinuities are used to show a break in a flight plan sequence and to keep a changed portion of a flight plan isolated from an unchanged portion during edits. They can be deleted using the DELETE command from the scratchpad or by inserting the next applicable waypoint. When deleted, a Direct-To course is created to the next waypoint. Some discontinuities, such as those before an approach with a radar-vectored initial leg, at the end of an airway where the next waypoint is not on that airway, or before a leg without a defined starting point, cannot be deleted with the DEL key.

Management of discontinuities on the LEGS page involves:
1. Entering the ACT/MOD LEGS page.
2. Pressing the DEL key or entering the next applicable waypoint into the scratchpad.
3. Pressing the LSK adjacent to the prompt boxes above the discontinuity.
4. Pressing the EXEC function key to confirm the change.

To remove legs following a discontinuity, select the applicable downtrack waypoint and enter it into the THEN prompt of the discontinuity, which will delete intermediate waypoints.

3. Pressing the LSK adjacent to the prompt boxes above the discontinuity.
4. Pressing the EXEC function key to confirm the change.

VNAV CLIMB is an ACT VNAV CLIMB page that shows when the aircraft is in the climb phase, allowing the pilot to specify or change a speed and altitude limit, a target speed, and the transition altitude/flight level.

If the preselect altitude is not raised to the flight plan target altitude or above, the preselected altitude will be captured, causing the mode to be sequenced to VALTS. VNAV will not sequence to climb VFLC until a climb mode selection is made (FLC, VS, or PTCH). When the aircraft approaches an altitude constraint, VNAV mode automatically sequences to VALTS or VALTV and remains in altitude hold until a climb is resumed. If the preselect altitude is not raised at least 45 s before reaching the constraint waypoint, CHECK PRESELECTOR message shows on the CDU. If the preselect altitude is raised before reaching the constraint waypoint, VNAV mode automatically sequences to VFLC and resumes the climb.
climb mode selection must be made (FLC, VS, or PTCH).

When a flight plan is created, the FMS automatically categorizes the first half of the waypoints as climbs (↑) and the last half as descents (↓). SID waypoints are assigned as climbs, and STAR and approach waypoints are assigned as descents.
Speed and Altitude Limit

amber altitude constraint during the climb phase indicates one of the following conditions: the current rate of climb is insufficient to meet the specified altitude constraints, all climb altitude constraints do not occur before all descent altitude constraints (except for the missed approach procedure), a climb altitude constraint is lower than the preceding climb altitude constraint, or an altitude constraint is higher than the Cruise Altitude.

The following conditions cause an altitude constraint to be displayed in amber during the climb phase:
- The current rate of climb or descent is not sufficient to meet the specified flight plan altitude constraints.
- All climb altitude constraints do not occur before all descent altitude constraints (except for the missed approach procedure).
- A climb altitude constraint is lower than the climb altitude constraint that comes before it.
- An altitude constraint is higher than the Cruise Altitude (CRZ ALT) that was defined on the PERF INIT page.

The VNAV CLIMB page displays the default setting for Target Speed, Transition Altitude, and Speed/Altitude Limit for the climb phase. Pilots can modify these settings as required, and data can be inputted for Speed/Altitude Limit if necessary.
On the VNAV CLIMB page, Indicated Airspeed (IAS) and Mach speeds are independent and can be set separately for each phase of flight.

Responses: The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft. It controls aircraft pitch, roll and thrust.

The Autoflight System manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path using information from the flight plan, FMS, radio navigation aids, or pilot inputs. It controls pitch, roll, and thrust via pitch, roll, and AT servos. The AT modes, integrated with vertical/lateral modes and the FMS, include Thrust Control, Speed Control, and Underspeed/Overspeed Protection, automatically selected based on active vertical modes.
It is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP).
Incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.

The Autoflight System has the following modes:
- Thrust Control Mode
- Speed Control Mode
- Underspeed and Overspeed Protection Mode
- Altitude Select Mode (ALTS Mode)
- Vertical Speed Mode (VS)
- Roll (ROLL) Mode
- APPR Mode - Lateral

The FLC Mode generates commands to hold the selected airspeed/Mach or the minimum vertical speed to achieve a preselected target altitude. When holding airspeed/Mach or minimum vertical speed, the FG generates a greater closure rate to reach the target altitude. It controls pitch to maintain commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed.

VNAV Mode allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints, providing references for altitude and speed. It ensures the aircraft flies in accordance with these constraints. VNAV is activated when enabled and valid, requiring the FMS as the navigation source with an active flight plan or a LOC source after NAV-to-NAV capture, and LNAV as the active lateral mode (or HDG within a predetermined deviation from the FMS flight plan). The FMS can automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS, or FLC modes based on flight plan constraints, or Path and Glidepath Modes for tracking vertical paths.

Or, the navigation source is FMS, and the active lateral Mode is HDG, but the aircraft's lateral flight path is within the predetermined deviation from the FMS flight plan.

The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft using information based on flight plan and data from the FMS, radio navigation aids, or manually entered data.
The AT Modes are integrated with the various vertical/lateral modes and the flight management system.
During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.

incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). When a vertical Mode is selected, incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.

The ALTS Mode is always armed, except when the ALT Mode, GS Mode or GA Mode is active. When the vertical Mode is GA, the ALTS Mode is armed if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft. When the ALT knob on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) is rotated, the ALTS Mode will be inhibited to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude change. The ALTS Mode is activated when the new attitude is selected or maintaining the current altitude.
The Altitude Hold (ALT) Mode maintains the aircraft at the currently selected altitude.
Hold preselected vertical speed.

The FLC Mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed, and generates commands to hold the selected airspeed/Mach or the minimum vertical speed, to achieve preselected target altitude.
VNAV Mode allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints and provides references for flying the aircraft in accordance with altitude and speed constraints.
The APPR Mode generates commands in the lateral axis to track and capture the selected navigation source (FMS/LOC/VOR).
The TO Mode can be used for the initiation of brake application during a rejected takeoff.
The GA Mode - Vertical guides the aircraft by holding the current heading of the aircraft.

The OSPD Mode activates to prevent the aircraft's speed from exceeding Vmo/Mmo by generating pitch commands to reduce airspeed. The USPD Mode activates to prevent stall by generating pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman.
The Windshear Escape (WS) Mode provides the optimal escape maneuver commands integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data until windshear warnings cease.

The Altitude Hold (ALT) Mode maintains the current altitude. It can be activated manually by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). It is also activated automatically when the preselected altitude changes during ALTS Mode activation or capture, or when VNAV Mode is deselected and ALTV Mode is activated, or when the FMS altitude is tracked in ALTV Mode. However, ALT Mode is inhibited if the APPR Mode is during GS capture. Pressing the ALT Button when ALT Mode is active will deselect it. After ALT Mode is activated, if no other vertical mode is selected, the aircraft will climb/descend due to inertia and then descend/climb again to capture the baro pressure altitude.
The ALT Mode can be deselected by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) or by activating other vertical modes.

The parallel offset function ensures that the aircraft is horizontally parallel offset according to the offset distance set by the crew along the original flight plan. While tracking an offset path, course heading and deviation are referenced to the offset path. Turn anticipation and waypoint alerts are also referenced from the offset intersections.

The vertical Mode, lateral Mode and AT Mode show on the FMA at the top of the PFD.

The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). When a vertical Mode is selected, the incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected. During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
Incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.

The Pitch (PTCH) Mode is engaged automatically when the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged for the first time, or if a lateral Mode is activated before a vertical Mode is selected. Engaging the AP when both FDs are disengaged also activates PTCH Mode. Selecting other vertical modes will deselect the PTCH Mode. Turning the PITCH/VS Wheel in Altitude Select (ALTS), Altitude Hold (ALT), Flight Level Change (FLC), Go-around (GA), PATH Angle, Glidepath (GP), or Overspeed (OSPD) (when not in overspeed status) modes will activate PTCH Mode and change the pitch angle reference. The PTCH Mode is the basic operating and default vertical mode of the AFCS.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode is always armed, except when ALT Mode, GS Mode, or GA Mode is active. The ALTS Mode is armed during GA Mode if the preselected altitude is 75 ft greater than the current altitude. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP inhibits ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes. The PTCH Mode is activated when the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged, or if no other vertical modes are selected. If ALTS Mode is activated and the preselected altitude is not adjusted, the FG is re-armed, ALTS Mode is activated, and PTCH Mode may appear but is immediately replaced by ALTS Mode.

The Vertical Speed (VS) Mode is selected by pressing the VS Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). In the VS Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the VS reference. The PITCH/VS Wheel is used to change the VS reference.

When the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged for the first time, or if a lateral Mode is activated before a vertical Mode is selected, or when both FDs are disengaged and the AP is engaged.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope. In APPR Mode, the AT controls airspeed.

The OSPD Mode is automatically activated when the aircraft Mach number is more than Mmo + 0.01, or the airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. In OSPD Mode, the system generates pitch commands to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt. The SPEED Knob is inhibited, and other vertical modes are inhibited unless in ALTS Mode, ALT Mode, TO Mode, or GA Mode. AT is armed in OSPD Mode.

The Underspeed (USPD) Mode automatically activates when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01. Its function is to provide pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman to prevent a stall.

The FD will first send a nose up command of 15° or below the Alpha Margin Indicator (AMI), whichever is lower. As the acceleration rate increases, the command bar is relatively far from AMI (pitch attitude not bigger than 2° ) to achieve a greater climb rate. After the windshear condition disappears, the command bar is 15° or slightly below AMI pitch attitude, whichever is lower.

Pilot-defined waypoints can be created in the following ways:
*   **Place Bearing/Distance (PBD) Waypoint:** Based on any valid geographically fixed point, defined by [IDENT][BRG]/[DIST/NAME].
*   **Along-Track Offset (ATO) Waypoint (also called Position/Distance (PD) Waypoint):** A point at a given distance before or after an existing waypoint along the route of flight, defined by [IDENT]/[DIST/NAME].
*   **Place Bearing/Place Bearing (PB/PB) Waypoint:** Defined by the intersection of two specified bearings from two base waypoints, defined by [IDENT][BRG]/[IDENT][BRG]/[NAME].
*   **Define and Store Pilot Waypoints:** Waypoints can be defined and stored on the DEFINE PILOT WPT page for future use. This involves entering a name, latitude and longitude, a PLACE BRG/DIST, or a PLACE BRG, and then pressing STORE WPT.
*   **Flyover Waypoint:** Any waypoint in the flight plan can be changed to a flyover waypoint by adding a "/0" after the waypoint identifier on the LEGS page.
*   **Direct-To Waypoint:** Waypoints can be entered directly into the flight plan by using the ACT DIRECT-TO page and entering the waypoint code.
*   **Select Pilot-Defined Waypoints:** Stored waypoints from the PILOT WPT LIST can be retrieved and inserted into the flight plan.

Responses: The Autoflight System controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft.

The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft using information based on flight plan and data from the FMS, radio navigation aids, or manually entered pilot data.
PFD
During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP).

The Autoflight System's vertical modes include Pitch (PTCH) Mode to hold a preselected pitch angle, Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode to capture a preselected barometric altitude, Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) to hold the current barometric altitude, Vertical Speed Mode (VS) to hold a preselected vertical speed, Flight Level Change (FLC) Mode to hold airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent, Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode for automatic selection of other vertical modes based on FMS commands, Approach (APPR) Mode - Glideslope (GS) Mode to descend according to glideslope or FMS commands, Takeoff (TO) Mode - Vertical for guidance based on takeoff target speed, Go-around (GA) Mode - Vertical for guidance based on go-around target speed, Overspeed (OSPD) Mode to hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number, Underspeed (USPD) Mode to hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number, and Windshear Escape Mode (WS) to hold a specified pitch angle and airspeed. The lateral modes include Roll (ROLL) Mode to hold aircraft heading or bank angle, 1/2 Bank (1/2 BANK) Mode to reduce the bank angle limit, Heading Select (HDG) Mode to hold a preselected heading, Lateral Navigation Mode (LNAV) to fly in accordance with navigation sources during en route flight, APPR Mode - Lateral to fly in accordance with navigation sources during approach, Takeoff (TO) Mode - Lateral to hold the aircraft's heading reference, and Go-around (GA) Mode - Lateral to hold the aircraft's current heading.
The purpose of the Autoflight System's Pitch (PTCH) Mode is to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at the time the mode is selected.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode captures a preselected barometric altitude, while the Altitude Hold (ALT) Mode maintains the current barometric altitude. The ALTS Mode responds to changes in barometric reference setting and uses the preselected altitude (or FMS target altitude if VNAV is active) as reference, whereas the ALT Mode does not respond to changes in barometric reference setting and holds the altitude at the moment of activation.
Hold airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent.

The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope.
Takeoff (TO) Mode - Vertical uses vertical guidance based on takeoff target speed, while Go-around (GA) Mode - Vertical uses vertical guidance based on go-around target speed.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is automatically activated when the aircraft Mach number is more than Mmo + 0.01, or the airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt, to prevent the aircraft speed from exceeding Vmo/Mmo by generating pitch commands to reduce airspeed. The Underspeed (USPD) Mode is automatically activated when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01, to prevent stall stick shaker by generating pitch commands to increase airspeed.

The Windshear Escape (WS) Mode is automatically entered by the Autoflight System when the TAWS detects a windshear warning. The system provides optimal escape maneuver commands integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data until the windshear warnings cease. The AP disengages automatically, and AT is set to TOGA thrust.

The Autoflight System's vertical, lateral, and AT modes are displayed on the FMA at the top of the PFD. It is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.

The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). When a vertical Mode is selected, the incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
Incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.

The Pitch (PTCH) Mode is activated automatically when the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged for the first time. It is also the default vertical mode if no other vertical modes are selected or if a lateral mode is activated before a vertical mode. Engaging the AP when both FDs are disengaged will also activate PTCH Mode. Selecting other vertical modes will deselect the PTCH Mode.
The ALTS Mode generates commands to capture or follow the preselected barometric altitude reference.
In the ALT Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to acquire and maintain the current pressure altitude.
In the VS Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the VS reference.
The FLC Mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed during climb or descent.

The VNAV Mode is engaged by pressing the VNAV Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). It is disengaged by pressing the VNAV Button, pressing the TOGA Pushbutton, changing the current navigation source, the glideslope being captured, or changing the FG coupled side.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope.

The TO Mode, when activated, provides pitch guidance of 15° for two-engine operation and 12° for one-engine operation after aircraft lift-off until the aircraft speed reaches the takeoff target speed. It also activates the FDs on both sides, displays them independently, sets the AT to takeoff thrust, and expands the pitch command upper limit of the FD to 30°.

In the roll axis, GA Mode commands are generated to hold the heading reference, with the flight guidance synchronizing the aircraft's heading to the existing heading. The bank angle is limited to ±5°. In the vertical axis, pitch angle is commanded to achieve the go-around target speed, with a lower pitch angle limit that starts at 8° and reduces to 4°. The pitch command upper limit for the flight director expands to 30°, while the autopilot's pitch control upper limit remains at 20°. The go-around target speed is the greater of VAPP and current speed, ranging from VREF + 5 kt to VREF + 20 kt during two-engine operation, and VREF + 5 kt to VREF + 15 kt during single-engine operation.
When overspeed occurs, the OSPD Mode is automatically activated and generates pitch commands to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo. The speed reference becomes Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt.

The Underspeed (USPD) Mode automatically activates when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman to prevent stall stick shaker.

The Windshear Escape (WS) Mode automatically engages when the TAWS detects a windshear warning, switching the lateral mode to GA and the vertical mode to WS. The Autopilot disengages after 2 seconds, and the system provides optimal escape maneuver commands integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data until windshear warnings cease. AT is set to TOGA thrust in WS Mode, and guidance commands are sent from one active Flight Director (FG).

The FMS Operations - Advanced Flight Plan chapter covers the creation and deletion of waypoints, including:
*   **Deleting any Waypoint:** Performed on the LEGS page by entering the page, pressing DEL LSK, then pressing the LSK adjacent to the waypoint to be deleted, and finally pressing EXEC.
*   **Deleting a Flyover Waypoint:** Performed on the LEGS page by entering the page, finding the flyover waypoint (suffixed with @), pressing CLR, pressing the LSK adjacent to the flyover waypoint, inputting "/0" to remove the flyover attribute, and then pressing the LSK for the waypoint again to insert the changed attribute, followed by EXEC.
*   **Deleting a Direct Waypoint:** Performed on the ACT/MOD FPLN page by entering the page, pressing DEL LSK, then pressing the TO LSK adjacent to the direct waypoint to be deleted.
*   **Creating a Flyover Waypoint:** Performed on the LEGS page by entering the page, clearing the scratchpad, pressing the LSK adjacent to the waypoint to be changed, inputting "/0" after the waypoint identifier, and then pressing the LSK for the waypoint identifier again to update the flight plan, followed by EXEC.

Discontinuities are used to show a break in a flight plan sequence or to keep a changed portion of a flight plan isolated from an unchanged portion. They can be deleted with a DELETE command from the scratchpad or by inserting the next applicable waypoint at the discontinuity prompt. Deleting a discontinuity creates a Direct-To course to the next waypoint. Some discontinuities, such as those before an approach with a radar-vectored initial leg, at the end of an airway where the next waypoint is not on that airway, or before a leg without a defined starting point (e.g., DME-arc), cannot be deleted with the DEL key. The operation to delete a discontinuity on the FPLN or LEGS page involves entering the ACT/MOD page, using the DEL command or selecting the next waypoint, pressing the LSK adjacent to the discontinuity, and then pressing EXEC. To remove legs following a discontinuity, the downtrack waypoint can be entered into the THEN prompt of the discontinuity, which replaces the discontinuity and deletes intermediate waypoints.

Responses: VNAV CLIMB
VNAV provides speed and altitude targets consistent with the climb constraints and speed limits, and automatic mode sequencing using the FLC mode (VFLC).

During the climb phase, VNAV allows the aircraft to climb to each specified constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. VNAV honors only climb constraints. If the altitude constraint requires crossing at a specific altitude, or at or below a specific altitude, that altitude is held until the waypoint is reached. If the constraint is between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If the constraint is at or above a specific altitude, no altitude holding is required. When approaching a constraint, VNAV updates the predicted altitude intercept; a violation triggers an UNABLE NEXT ALT message. If an altitude change mode is selected while at a constraint altitude and the preselected altitude is raised, VNAV allows leaving the constraint. However, for AT, AT OR BELOW, or BETWEEN constraints, CHECK FPLN ALT is displayed. Upon reaching capture distance, VNAV automatically sequences to an altitude hold mode (VALTS, VALTV, or VALT). BOC (Bottom of Climb) is shown 1 minute before reaching the waypoint, and the FPTA changes. If the preselect altitude is not raised 45 seconds before the waypoint, CHECK PRESELECTOR is displayed.

When the aircraft is within capture distance of a constraint altitude during a climb, VNAV automatically sequences to VALTS, VALTV, or VALT and remains in that mode until a climb is resumed. The PFD will show an altitude capture. If the capture altitude differs from the preselect altitude, an aural alert sounds when within 1000 ft of capture. If the preselect altitude is not raised at least 45 seconds before reaching the constraint waypoint, a CHECK PRESELECTOR message appears on the CDU. At 5 seconds before the bottom of the climb, BOC flashes and a VNAV aural alert sounds. If the preselect altitude is raised before reaching the constraint, VNAV sequences to VFLC and resumes the climb after crossing the waypoint.

During a climb, VNAV allows the aircraft to climb to each specified constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. Responses: The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft.

The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft. It consists of two Flight Guides (FGs), two Flight Directors (FDs), one Autopilot (AP), one Autothrottle (AT), and three Yaw Dampers (YDs). It also includes a Mach Trim function. The system manages pitch, roll, and thrust via its servo mechanisms and displays its status and modes on the PFD.
The Autoflight System's vertical, lateral, and Autothrottle (AT) modes are displayed on the FMA, located in the upper area of the PFD.

The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). When a vertical Mode is selected, the incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
When a vertical Mode is selected, the incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.

When the PTCH Mode is activated, the FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at the time of mode selection. The PITCH/VS Wheel is then used to change the pitch angle reference, which can range from -15° to 20°. The AT controls airspeed in PTCH Mode.

The Altitude Hold (ALT) Mode can be activated manually by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) or automatically. In ALT Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to acquire and maintain the current pressure altitude. The Autothrottle (AT) controls airspeed in this mode.

The Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints, providing references for altitude and speed. It is engaged by pressing the VNAV Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP).
In OSPD Mode, the system generates pitch commands as required to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo. The speed reference is Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt.
When overspeed occurs, the OSPD Mode is automatically activated except if either ALTS Mode or ALT Mode are activated or GS Mode is captured.

The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft using information from the flight plan and data from the FMS, radio navigation aids, or pilot input. It utilizes pitch and roll servos, along with an Autothrottle (AT), to manage pitch, roll, and thrust. The Flight Guidance (FG) system calculates and sends pitch and roll commands to the Autopilot (AP) and Flight Director (FD), and also provides commands to the AT and Yaw Dampers (YD). The AP then uses pitch and roll servos to control the aircraft's attitude according to the FG's commands. The AT receives input from various systems to provide automatic thrust control.

The Autoflight System provides windshear recovery guidance by sending calculated pitch and roll maneuver commands. After the TAWS sends a windshear warning, the FD will first send a nose-up command of 15° or below the Alpha Margin Indicator (AMI), whichever is lower. If the AT is engaged, the thrust levers will automatically advance to the TO/GA detent. Then, the FD sends a command of nose-up for not more than 2° from the stick shaker (Alpha Margin Indicator (AMI) indication). At low altitude, the command bar is closer to AMI to expect a bigger climb rate. As the acceleration rate increases, the command bar is relatively far from AMI (pitch attitude not bigger than 2°) to achieve a greater climb rate. After the windshear condition disappears, the command bar is 15° or slightly below AMI pitch attitude, whichever is lower. In WS Mode, AT is set to TOGA thrust.

Responses: Stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) is engaged when the aircraft is in flight and close to stall. This results in the engagement of both stick shakers, an aural "Stall, Stall, ......" alert, and a red warning flag on the PFDs. The stick shaker continuously jitters as long as the Angle of Attack (AOA) is above its threshold. If the AOA continues to increase beyond the stick shaker level, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) automatically sends a push command to the pitch servo, activating the stick pusher to prevent a stall.

Responses: The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll, and thrust via the pitch servo, roll servo, and AT servo.

The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll, and thrust via the pitch servo, roll servo, and AT servo. The vertical Mode, lateral Mode, and AT Mode are displayed on the FMA at the top of the PFD.
cognize and understand the active and armed Mod

The vertical Mode, lateral Mode and AT Mode show on the FMA at the top of the PFD. During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
When a mode is selected, the related mode annunciations will show on the FMA at the top of the PFD.

The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch via the pitch servo and the AP pitch servo, which drives the pitch and roll servos based on commands from the FG. The AP pitch servo is installed on the left elevator module and moves the control column in accordance with pitch servo action when the AP is engaged. The AP pitch control is limited between 20° nose up and -15° nose down. In Pitch (PTCH) Mode, the FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle. The PITCH/VS Wheel is used to change the reference of pitch angle, with a range of -15° to 20°.

When the aircraft is in the ALTS Mode, the FG generates commands to capture or follow the preselected barometric altitude reference. If VNAV is not engaged, the FG uses the altitude preselected by the ALT Knob on the FCP. If VNAV is activated, the FMS target altitude can also be used as a reference. The FG compares the altitude with the FCP preselected altitude and uses the closest altitude as the reference. The AT controls airspeed in ALTS Mode.

The FLC Mode generates commands to hold the selected airspeed/Mach or the minimum vertical speed to achieve a preselected target altitude. When holding the airspeed/Mach reference or the minimum vertical speed, the Flight Guidance (FG) system generates a greater closure rate to reach the target altitude. If the preselected altitude changes in the active FLC Mode, the FLC Mode climbs or descends toward the new preselected altitude. Once the aircraft reaches the target altitude, the FG will automatically change into the Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode.

When VNAV is activated, the Flight Guidance (FG) system compares the aircraft's altitude with both the FMS target altitude and the preselected altitude on the Flight Control Panel (FCP), using the altitude closest to the aircraft as the reference.

The Go-around (GA) Mode is used to initiate a go-around maneuver. When activated, it commands pitch angle according to go-around target speed and holds the heading reference in the roll axis with a bank angle limit of ±5°.

Both OSPD and USPD modes are automatically activated when overspeed or underspeed conditions occur, respectively, to maintain aircraft speed within safe limits. In both modes, the Autopilot (AP) provides pitch commands and the Autothrottle (AT) provides thrust/speed commands. Upon exiting these modes, the system typically transitions to FLC Mode.

The Windshear Escape (WS) Mode in the Autoflight System is automatically engaged by the TAWS when a windshear warning is detected. Its purpose is to provide optimal escape maneuver commands by integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data. The system disengages the Autopilot automatically and sets Thrust to TOGA. The WS Mode continues until windshear warnings cease. To exit the WS Mode, the pilot must manually select any other vertical mode.
The Windshear Escape (WS) Mode is automatically entered when the TAWS detects a windshear warning.
Manually press the TOGA Pushbutton or select any other vertical modes.

To manually exit the WS Mode, selection of another vertical mode is required. Once the windshear warning ceases, the system exits the WS Mode and the TAWS sends windshear warning. Manually press the TOGA Pushbutton, and the system transfers to the standard GA Mode. If the windshear warning no longer exists, selection of another vertical mode will cancel WS mode.

The FLC Mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed, and when an altitude constraint or preselect altitude is encountered during a climb, the altitude is captured and held using an altitude hold mode. Once the aircraft reaches the target altitude, the FG will automatically change into the ALTS Mode.

VNAV Mode allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints and provides references for these modes. It provides automatic mode sequencing using FLC mode that shows as VFLC on the PFD. It also provides speed and altitude targets consistent with the climb constraints and speed limits.

The USPD mode is a vertical mode that automatically activates when the aircraft's airspeed drops below Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01 M, unless ALTS mode is captured or ALT mode is active. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. When the airspeed exceeds Vman/Mman, USPD mode deactivates automatically and the vertical mode switches to FLC Mode. Other vertical modes are inhibited when USPD mode is active, except for ALTS Mode, ALT Mode, TO Mode, and GA Mode.

Responses: The wheel brake system includes: Normal Brake System, Park/emergency brake system, and Brake temperature monitoring system.

The wheel brake system includes the Normal Brake System (Manual and autobrake modes), the Park/emergency brake system (Emergency and parking brake modes), and the Brake temperature monitoring system. The system is electrically controlled and hydraulically actuated by the Brake Control Unit (BCU). No. 1 hydraulic system charges the Inboard Brake Accumulator for inboard wheel brakes, and No. 2 hydraulic system charges the Outboard Brake Accumulator for outboard wheel brakes. Check valves prevent backflow from accumulators. Brake accumulators can supply pressure to the emergency brake even with hydraulic system failure, providing six full brake applications. The main wheels have fusible plugs to prevent tire bursting due to overheating, and nose and main wheels have tire overpressure relief valves. Wear pins indicate brake wear, and temperature sensors on each brake send data to the BCU for EICAS display.

The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the refueling process and automatically controls the Refuel Shutoff Valve to close when fuel in the tank reaches the preselected quantity. With an imbalance of more than 400 kg (882 lb), the tank with the higher quantity will be shutoff. When the tanks are balanced, both tanks will be refueled.

In manual refueling mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to MANUAL, allowing refueling personnel to open and close the Refuel Shutoff Valve via the TANK REFUELING Switch. This manual shutoff function overrides the automatic shutoff. In automatic refueling mode, with the REFUEL SELECTION Switch set to AUTO, the Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the process and automatically controls the Refuel Shutoff Valve to close when the preselected quantity is reached.

The manual shutoff function overrides the automatic shutoff function by allowing refueling personnel to manually open and close the Refuel Shutoff Valve via the TANK REFUELING Switch on the Refuel/defuel Control Panel. Even under automatic refueling mode, refueling can be stopped by manually setting the TANK REFUELING Switch to CLOSE.

The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the refueling process and automatically controls the Refuel Shutoff Valve to close when fuel in the tank reaches the preselected quantity. It also automatically records the last preselected refuel quantity and ensures that fuel quantities between the left and right fuel tanks are balanced.

In automatic refueling mode, the Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) balances fuel quantities between the left and right fuel tanks by shutting off the refuel shutoff valve in the tank with the higher quantity if an imbalance of more than 400 kg (882 lb) occurs. Once the tanks are balanced, both refuel shutoff valves are opened to complete the refueling process simultaneously.

Bleed air is adjusted by two PACKs for temperature and pressure. This air then enters the mixing manifold and is combined with recirculated air from the cabin. Recirculation filters on the lower side of the cabin filter the air before it's extracted by two recirculation fans, part of which is sent to the mixing manifold.

In emergency situations, such as when both PACKs fail and the flight altitude is below 10000 ft with CAB ΔP less than 1 psi, the flight crew can activate the emergency RAM air system using the RAM AIR Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel. This allows outside air to enter the mixing manifold.
The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and the recirculation fans and is supplied with ground air conditioning through a low pressure ground connection.

The temperature of the air distributed to the cockpit and cabin is controlled by mixing hot trim air from upstream of the PACK with air from the mixing manifold, which contains fresh cold air from the PACK and recirculated air from the cabin.
The two recirculation fans can be manually disabled by releasing the RECIRC Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel, which results in the fans being OFF.

The temperature of the cockpit and cabin are controlled independently by the integrated air system controllers. The pilot sets the cockpit and cabin temperature by adjusting the temperature knob on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel.
The trim air pressure regulating valve is pneumatically actuated and electrically controlled.

The trim air valves deliver hot air flow to the cockpit and cabin distribution ducts to achieve the temperature requirements of these areas. They are electrically controlled and operated by the integrated air system controllers.
If electrical power is lost, they remain in current position.

Responses: tall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functio
Two Angle of Attack (AOA) Sensors integrated with Stall Protection Computers (SPC), one stick pusher integrated in AP pitch servo, and two stick shakers.

There are two Stall Protection Computers (SPCs). Each SPC can independently initiate stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition. They complete independent computations. The stick pusher activates only when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands simultaneously.
tall alert, stall protection and auto-ignitio

The Stall Protection System (SPS) includes two Angle of Attack (AOA) Sensors integrated with Stall Protection Computers (SPCs). Each SPC independently computes stall alerts. When AOA exceeds a threshold, the SPC can initiate stall protection. If AOA continues to increase after stick shaker activation, the SPC commands the AP pitch servo to activate the stick pusher. Each SPC can drive both stick shakers, and the stick pusher is activated only when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands simultaneously.

The stick pusher is activated when the A/P-A/T-S/P DISC Switch on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) is in the up position and the aircraft is in a condition that triggers stall protection, or when the STALL ADVANCE Switch on the overhead panel is pushed, enhancing the stall protection margin.

The context provided does not contain information about functions initiated when the Angle of Attack (AOA) exceeds a threshold.

Stall protection commands are sent by the Stall Protection System (SPS). The stick pusher activates when the SPS is in ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 1, Ice Advance Mode 2, Ice Advance Mode 3, or Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode, and the AOA threshold for these modes is met.
The modes associated with stick pusher activation in the Stall Protection System (SPS) are normal Mode, Advance On Mode, Ice Advance Mode 1, Ice Advance Mode 2, and Ice Advance Mode 3.

The priority of the Stall Protection System (SPS) modes reduces in the sequence: Flap/Slat System Fail Advance Mode, ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 3, Ice Advance Mode 2, Ice Advance Mode 1, and normal Mode. Compared to normal mode, the AOA threshold for stall alert, stall protection stick pusher, and auto-ignition decreases in all other modes.

The AOA of stall alert and stick pusher is the same between Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2. It's also the same between Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode. However the AOA of the former (Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2) is greater than that of the latter one (Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode).
Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2

The context states that "the AOA of stall alert and stick pusher is the same between Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2" and that "the AOA of the former (Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2) is greater than that of the latter one (Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode)." However, it does not provide the specific numerical AOA thresholds for these modes.

DVANCE ON Mode activates if the STALL ADVANCE Switch is pushed, and the ON light illuminates.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) enters Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode in any of the following conditions:
- Flap system fails on FSECU bus, and flap configuration is not in 0.
- Flap system fails on FSECU bus or slat angle on both sides is not available, and flap configuration is not in 0.
- The slat angle difference between the two sides is 3° for 5 s, and flap configuration is not in 0.

When the conditions for Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode, ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 3, Ice Advance Mode 2, or Ice Advance Mode 1 are not satisfied. However, Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 2 has a different rule where it will remain active even if its conditions are not satisfied, unless a higher priority mode is triggered.
No
To exit Ice Advance Mode 2: When flap is down and aircraft is in level flight, cycle the STALL ADVANCE Switch.

Ice Advance Mode 2 cannot exit automatically. It remains active even after the WING A/I Switch is disconnected, and can only be exited manually by cycling the STALL ADVANCE Switch when the flap is down and the aircraft is in level flight.

Cycling the STALL ADVANCE Switch, when flap is down and the aircraft is in level flight, will cause the Stall Protection System (SPS) to exit Ice Advance Mode 2. The SPS ICE MODE 2 message will disappear from the EICAS display.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) calculates the AOA threshold for stall alert, stall protection and automatic ignition based on the STALL ADVANCE Switch. When the aircraft is on the ground and airspeed is below 80 knots, stall alert, stall protection stick pusher and auto-ignition functions are inhibited.

The stick pusher is activated by the Stall Protection System when the A/P-A/T-S/P DISC Switch is in the up position, restoring stick pusher function. The stick pusher can also be inhibited temporarily by pressing the AP/SP DISC Pushbutton on the control wheel during activation, after which it will resume its action based on the current condition. Stall alert, stall protection stick pushing, and auto-ignition are lost when both left and right stall protection computers fail.
DVANCE ON Mod

Compared to normal mode, the threshold value for stall alert, stall protection stick pusher and auto-ignition AOA in other modes decrease. The Advance On Mode, drives the stall alert (stick vibration, STALL aural alert and the warning flag on the PFD). The stick pusher reduces when the AOA returns to normal condition, this enhances the stall protection margin. The AOA of stall alert and stick pusher is the same between Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2. It's also the same between Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode. However the AOA of the former (Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2) is greater than that of the latter one (Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode). SPS ICE MODE 2 message on EICAS display disappears when Ice Advance Mode 2 is exited. To exit Ice Advance Mode 2: When flap is down and aircraft is in level flight, cycle the STALL ADVANCE Switch.

Responses: The Air conditioning system is fully automatic and is controlled and monitored by two Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs). It adjusts bleed air via the PACKs to condition air for the cabin, cockpit, avionics, and cargo compartments, with exhaust air discharged through the outflow valve.

The air conditioning system adjusts bleed air via the PACKs, which then adjusts temperature and pressure. This conditioned air is then mixed with recirculated air from the cabin in the mixing manifold. Hot trim air is further mixed with the air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct before being distributed to the cockpit and cabin.
Hot trim air from upstream of the PACK is mixed with air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct, and then distributed to the cockpit and cabin.
The exhaust air is discharged via the outflow valve.

The air conditioning system adjusts bleed air via the PACKs, and this conditioned air is ducted to the cabin, cockpit, avionics compartment, and cargo compartment. Exhaust air is discharged via the outflow valve. On the ground, an external ground air conditioning unit can supply conditioned air to the mixing manifold for cabin ventilation.

The bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted through two flow control valves and its temperature and pressure are adjusted through two PACKs. It is then mixed with recirculated cabin air in a mixing manifold. Hot trim air from upstream of the PACK is further mixed with this air in the air conditioning distribution duct, and then distributed to the cockpit and cabin.
mixing manifold
Hot trim air from the upstream of the PACK
The mixed air is distributed to the cockpit and cabin to maintain selected temperature.

On the lower side of the cabin, the air is filtered by recirculation filters and extracted from the cabin by two recirculation fans. Part of the recirculated air is sent to the mixing manifold to mix with the fresh cold air from the PACK, and the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
Part of the recirculated air is sent to the mixing manifold to mix with the fresh cold air from the PACK, and the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
The integrated air system controllers regulate the flow control valves to automatically control the air conditioning flow.
The Integrated Air System Controllers regulate the cabin ventilation and temperature, and control the outflow valve and ground valve.
The integrated air system controllers regulate the flow control valves to control shutoff and overheat protection of bleed air, temperature regulation, and flow monitoring.

When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft. When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi, with fresh air provided through the emergency RAM air valve.
The flow control valves can be closed by turning off the L(R) PACK Switch on the AIR CONTROL Control Panel.

The autobrake system has two operating modes: landing mode for initiating brake application during landing, and takeoff mode for initiating brake application during a rejected takeoff. It also provides antiskid protection, crossover protection, and touchdown protection during its operation.
antiskid protection, crossover protection and touchdown protectio

The autobrake takeoff mode is armed when all Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground, the wheel speed is below 55 kt, and the brake system does not detect a fault. The autobrake landing mode is armed when the autobrake is set to LO, MED, or HI, the WOW signals indicate the aircraft is in flight, and the brake system does not detect a fault.

The autobrake system is disarmed when: the brake system detects a fault; the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than the selected mode (RTO for takeoff, OFF for landing); one or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate the aircraft is in flight (for takeoff mode) or on the ground (for landing mode); there is an "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU); or the WOW signals disagree. For takeoff mode, it is also disarmed when the brake pedal application is 25% greater than the total application available or when any thrust lever is pushed forward beyond IDLE. For landing mode, it is also disarmed when the ground spoilers are retracted.

Takeoff Mode: When the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to RTO, and all Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground, the wheel speed is below 55 kt, and the brake system does not detect a fault.
Landing Mode: When the autobrake is set (LO, MED and HI), and the Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight, and the brake system does not detect a fault.
Takeoff mode is used for the initiation of brake application during a rejected takeoff. Landing Mode is used for the initiation of brake application during landing.

The autobrake system disarms during braking if the brake system detects a fault, the AUTOBRAKE Selector is not in RTO (for landing mode), brake pedal application is 25% greater than total application, one or more WOW signals indicate the aircraft is in flight, or any thrust lever is pushed forward beyond IDLE. In landing mode, retraction of ground spoilers also causes disarm.

The wheel brake system detects a fault, the AUTOBRAKE Selector is not in RTO, the application of any brake pedal is 25 % greater than the total application available and lasts for 1 s, one or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight, or any thrust lever is pushed forward to a position greater than IDLE.

The autobrake system is enabled when the wheel speed is above 60 kt and the Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground.

Takeoff Mode:
- The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than RTO.
- One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight.
- The brake system detects a fault.
- An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU).

Landing Mode:
- The same conditions that cause the autobrake to disarm after arming occur. (The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to OFF, the brake system detects a fault, an "arm disagree" between the two channels of the BCU, or WOW signals disagree.)
The autobrake system operates when two thrust levers are in IDLE or reverser position and the AUTOBRAKE Selector is in RTO, or when all conditions for landing mode application are met for 3 seconds.

During autobrake operation, the autobrake will disarm in any of the following conditions:
- The brake system detects a fault.
- The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than RTO (for takeoff mode) or OFF or RTO (for landing mode).
- One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight.
- An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU).
- The Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals received by the wheel brake system disagree.
- The application of any brake pedal is 25 % greater than the total application available and lasts for 1 s (for takeoff mode) or is 25 % greater than the total application available (for landing mode).
- Any thrust lever is pushed forward to a position greater than IDLE (for takeoff mode) or pushed forward than IDLE (for landing mode).
- The ground spoilers are retracted from the extended position (for landing mode).

TCAS comprises the following components: a transponder, a display (PFD/MFD), and an audio alert system.
TCAS interrogates other aircraft ATC transponders to determine their relative bearing, range, closure rate, and relative altitude.
Its relative bearing, its range and closure rate, and its relative altitude.
the intruder trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) and the estimated time (TAU) to reach the CP

When the relative position of the intruder presents a collision threat, aural and visual alerts are triggered. TCAS optimizes vertical orders to ensure sufficient trajectory separation and a variable minimal vertical speed considering all intruders.

TCAS classifies intruder aircraft based on proximity, potential for collision, and time to Closest Point of Approach (CPA). This classification includes "Proximate traffic" (no collision threat), "Traffic Advisory (TA)" (potential collision threat with TAU ~40s), and "Resolution Advisory (RA)" (real collision threat with TAU ~25s).
Proximate Traffic is displayed as a filled cyan diamond.

Traffic Advisory (TA) informs the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when conditions change. The associated Time to Closest Point of Approach (TAU) is about 40 seconds.
Traffic Advisory (TA) is indicated by a filled amber circle on the TCAS display. An aural alert will also sound when a TA occurs.
Resolution Advisory (RA) is a "Real collision threat" and has a typical Time to Closest Point of Approach (TAU) of about 25 seconds.

Resolution Advisory (RA) is indicated by a filled red box on the vertical speed scale of the PFD, accompanied by an aural alert. Vertical speed orders for RA are displayed on the vertical speed scale on the PFD, indicating either to maintain current V/S (PRA) or to modify V/S (CRA).
Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA) and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA)
"Other Traffic" is displayed as a filled cyan diamond.
The different classifications of intruder alerts in TCAS are: Proximate traffic, Traffic Advisory (TA), and Resolution Advisory (RA).

Traffic Advisory (TA) informs the pilot of proximate traffic that does not currently constitute a threat but may become one if conditions change. It is indicated to the pilot as a filled amber circle on the TCAS display.
void deviation from the present vertical flight path.

– Traffic Advisory (TA): Potential collision threat, TAU is about 40s.
– Resolution Advisory (RA): Real collision threat, TAU is about 25s. RAs are further categorized into Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA) and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA).
Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA) warns the pilot to take actions, such as climb or descent, to avoid threat aggravation.

TCAS alerts will be inhibited below 1100 ft AGL during climb or below 900 ft AGL during descent for certain RA limits, below 1200 ft AGL during climb or below 1000 ft AGL during descent for other RA limits, and below 1650 ft AGL during climb or below 1450 ft AGL during descent for accelerated RA descent.

TCAS RAs are inhibited below 1100 ft AGL during climb or below 900 ft AGL during descent, or below 1200 ft AGL during climb or below 1000 ft AGL during descend depending on the RA limit. For a descent rate of 1500 ft/min, RAs are inhibited below 1650 ft AGL during climb or below 1450 ft AGL during descend.

The two CDUs are located on the central pedestal and provide basic control and display of the FMS for the flight crew. They are capable of supporting data pages with 14 lines of 24 characters, with line 14 serving as a scratchpad line. Line 15 is an annunciation line for messages requiring crew attention. Line Select Keys (LSKs) are used to copy or transfer data to/from the scratchpad, or to select a mode of operation or function related to the display page.

*   Copy or transfer data in the scratchpad to the line.
*   Copy or transfer data in the line to the scratchpad.
*   Select a mode of operation or function related to the display page.
*   Execute the related function.

Responses: Mode 1 is Excessive Rate of Descent. When CPA is inoperative and the current sink rate is excessive, a reactive mid-term caution and a reactive short-term warning will be triggered depending on radio altitude and vertical speed. Entering the amber caution envelope triggers the "SINK RATE" aural alert, and entering the red warning envelope triggers the "WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP" aural alert.

When the Collision Prediction Alerting (CPA) is inoperative and the current sink rate is excessive, a reactive mid-term caution will be triggered when the aircraft enters the amber caution envelope, activating the SINK RATE aural alert. A reactive short-term warning will be triggered when the aircraft enters the red warning envelope, activating the WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP aural alert. These alerts are dependent on radio altitude and vertical speed.

In Mode 1 (Excessive Rate of Descent), a "SINK RATE" aural alert activates when the aircraft enters the amber caution envelope, and a "WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP" aural alert sounds when it enters the red warning envelope. These alerts are triggered when the Collision Prediction Alerting (CPA) is inoperative and the current sink rate is excessive, depending on radio altitude and vertical speed.

- **Mode 1: Excessive Rate of Descent:**
    - Triggers: Excessive sink rate when CPA is inoperative.
    - Alerts:
        - Amber caution envelope: SINK RATE
        - Red warning envelope: WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP
- **Mode 2: Excessive Rate of Terrain Closure Rate:**
    - Triggers: Excessive closure rate between track and terrain when CPA is inoperative, dependent on radio altitude, indicated airspeed, landing gear, and flap configuration.
    - Alerts:
        - Caution: TERRAIN TERRAIN
        - Warning: WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP
- **Mode 4: Incorrect Landing Configuration:**
    - Triggers: Incorrect landing configuration with insufficient terrain clearance, dependent on radio altitude, landing gear, flap configuration, and airspeed.
    - Alerts: TOO LOW TERRAIN, TOO LOW GEAR, or TOO LOW FLAPS
- **Mode 5: Excessive Deviation From G/S:**
    - Triggers: Excessive deviation below the G/S with landing gear down, dependent on radio altitude, G/S deviation, LOC deviation, landing gear configuration, and G/S inhibit signals.
    - Alerts: GLIDE SLOPE (volume and frequency increase with deviation and decreasing altitude).
- **Mode 7: Reactive Windshear Detection:**
    - Triggers: Hazardous microbursts/windshear events with similar characteristics at low altitude, identified by monitoring wind parameters affecting aircraft performance. Also triggers when windshear improves aircraft performance.
    - Alerts: Aural alert notifying flight crew of degraded aircraft performance or awareness of potentially degrading windshear.
TOO LOW FLAPS, GLIDE SLOPE

- Mode 5: Excessive Deviation From G/S: Can be inhibited manually via the TAWS G/S switch. It is automatically inhibited if the angle between runway heading and track orientation is more than 90°, LOC deviation is more than 3 dots, or the landing gear is not extended.

Responses: The main components of the air conditioning process are the PACKs, mixing manifold, and recirculation fans.

Bleed air enters the PACKs, where its temperature and pressure are adjusted. From the PACKs, air enters the mixing manifold, where it is combined with recirculated air filtered by recirculation fans. Hot trim air is then mixed with the air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct for cabin and cockpit distribution.

The integrated air system controllers control the PACKs. The recirculation fans are controlled by the RECIRC Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel. The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and recirculation fans.

When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft. When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi, allowing for fresh air through the emergency RAM air valve.

When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi. Sufficient fresh air can be provided to the cockpit and cabin through the emergency RAM air valve when these conditions are satisfied.

The flight crew can open the emergency RAM air valve with the RAM AIR Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel.

The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and the recirculation fans and distributes it to the cabin. It also receives air from the emergency RAM air valve and the low pressure ground connection.

Bleed air is adjusted by flow control valves and PACKs for temperature and pressure, then mixed with recirculated cabin air in the mixing manifold. Hot trim air is added in the air conditioning distribution duct before being sent to the cockpit and cabin. In the AFT cargo compartment, part of the recirculated air ventilates it and is exhausted to the cargo triangular area. Cargo shutoff valves isolate the compartment in case of fire.
Part of the recirculated air is sent to the mixing manifold to mix with the fresh cold air from the PACK, and the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.

The air conditioning flow is automatically controlled by the integrated air system controllers, which regulate the flow control valves. Bleed air enters the mixing manifold, where it is mixed with recirculated air from the cabin. Hot trim air from upstream of the PACK is then mixed with the air from the mixing manifold. Recirculated air is filtered, and part is sent to the mixing manifold, while the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
hutoff and overheat protection of bleed air, temperature regulation of air conditioning system and flow monitoring

The air conditioning flow is automatically controlled by the integrated air system controllers, which regulate the flow control valves. The air conditioning system is fully automatic and is controlled and monitored by two Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs).

The air conditioning system has built-in-test and failure detection functions. Each integrated air system controller has two channels (A and B) that are crosslinked for switching and monitoring. If the active channel fails, the standby channel takes over automatically. Each channel has an independent power supply. If one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operation, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft. If both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft with cabin differential pressure less than 1 psi, and emergency RAM air can be used.
The flow control valves can be closed by turning off the L(R) PACK Switch on the AIR CONTROL Panel.

Responses: TCAS functions include: Detecting aircraft equipped with transponders, displaying potential and predicted collision targets, and issuing vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflict. It is independent of ground-based ATC and has a detection range of 30-40 NM laterally and 9900 ft vertically.

TCAS is independent of the ground-based ATC. TCAS constantly interrogates other aircraft ATC transponders and determines their relative bearing, range, closure rate, and relative altitude. It then computes intruder trajectories, Closest Point of Approach (CPA), and estimated time to CPA. When a collision threat is presented, TCAS triggers aural and visual alerts and issues vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflict.

TCAS detects aircraft within a maximum lateral range of 30 NM – 40 NM and a maximum altitude range of 9900 ft. TCAS determines the intruder's relative bearing, range and closure rate, and relative altitude (ATC mode C or S).
One TCAS receiver/transmitter, Two TCAS directional antennas.

the intruder trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach ( CPA ) and the estimated time (TAU ) to reach the CPA.
When the relative position of the intruder presents a collision threat, aural and visual alerts are triggered.
Traffic Advisory (TA), Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA), and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA).

Traffic Advisories (TAs) inform the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when conditions change. TCAS detects aircraft equipped with transponders flying within a maximum lateral range of 30-40 NM and within 9900 ft above/below the aircraft. TCAS determines the intruder's relative bearing, range, closure rate, and relative altitude. It then computes the intruder trajectory, Closest Point of Approach (CPA), and estimated time to reach CPA.

Traffic Advisory (TA) informs the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when conditions change. The estimated time to Closest Point of Approach (TAU) for a TA is about 40 seconds.

Resolution Advisory (RA) defines a real collision threat, with an estimated time to Closest Point of Approach (TAU) of about 25 s.

Resolution Advisories (RAs) are displayed as a filled red box on the vertical speed scale of the PFD, accompanied by an aural alert. They warn the pilot to take actions (such as climb or descent) to avoid threat aggravation.
Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA) and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA)

TCAS classifies intruders into the following categories:
*   **Proximate traffic:** No collision threat, in adjacent airspace, closer than 6 NM laterally and ±1200 ft vertically. Displayed as an unfilled cyan diamond on the PFD/MFD.
*   **Traffic Advisory (TA):** Potential collision threat, TAU is about 40 s. Displayed as a filled amber circle on the PFD/MFD, with aural messages.
*   **Resolution Advisory (RA):** Real collision threat, TAU is about 25 s. Displayed as a filled red box on the PFD/MFD. Aural messages are provided, and vertical speed orders are displayed on the PFD's vertical speed scale to maintain the current V/S (preventive resolution advisory - PRA) or modify V/S (corrective resolution advisory - CRA).
*   **Other Traffic:** No collision threat, non-proximate traffic within the surveillance envelope. Displayed as an unfilled cyan diamond on the PFD/MFD.

- **Resolution Advisory (RA):** Real collision threat (TAU ~ 25s). Displayed as a filled red box on PFD/MFD with aural messages and vertical maneuvering orders on the PFD.
- **Other Traffic:** No collision threat, optional display of non-proximate traffic within surveillance envelope. Displayed as an unfilled cyan diamond on PFD/MFD.

If the aircraft is not on an intercept heading to the selected navigation source, or the selected navigation source is invalid, the LNAV Mode is armed, and the FG operates in HDG Mode.

The LNAV Mode is selected by pressing the LNAV Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). When the LNAV Mode is active, the system generates commands to capture and track the selected navigation source (FMS/LOC/VOR). If the aircraft is not on an intercept heading to the selected navigation source, or the selected navigation source is invalid, the LNAV Mode is armed, and the FG operates in HDG Mode. If the aircraft is on an intercept heading to the selected course, LNAV Mode is activated, and the HDG Mode is deselected. The LNAV Mode activates without delay if the VOR/LOC deviation is minimum at the time of selection. The system operates in Dead Reckoning Mode during VOR station overfly. The LNAV Mode can be deselected by changing the active navigation source, changing the frequency of the navigation source, changing the FG coupled side, or selecting other lateral modes.

When the Collision Prediction Alerting (CPA) is inoperative and the current sink rate is excessive, a mid-term caution and a short-term warning are triggered based on radio altitude and vertical speed. Entering the amber caution envelope activates the "SINK RATE" aural alert, while entering the red warning envelope triggers the "WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP" aural alert.

- SINK RATE: When the aircraft enters the amber caution envelope in Mode 1 of the Reactive Alert Function.
- WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP: When the aircraft enters the red warning envelope in Mode 1 of the Reactive Alert Function.

- Amber caution envelope: SINK RATE aural alert
- Red warning envelope: WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP aural alert

Mode 2: Excessive Rate of Terrain Closure Rate. When the Collision Prediction Alerting (CPA) is inoperative and the closure rate between the current track and terrain is excessive, a caution or warning will be triggered according to radio altitude, indicated airspeed, landing gear configuration and flap configuration. When a mode 2 caution is triggered, TERRAIN TERRAIN aural alert will sound. When a mode 2 warning is triggered, WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP aural alert will sound.

Mode 7: Reactive Windshear Detection. TAWS has reactive windshear detection capability, active during takeoff and approach. It identifies hazardous microbursts and/or similar windshear events at low altitude by monitoring wind parameters that affect aircraft performance. If aircraft performance degrades to a predetermined threshold, TAWS triggers an aural alert to notify the crew of degraded performance and proximity to a hazardous condition. It also triggers an alert when windshear improves performance, providing awareness that degrading performance windshear could be encountered.

TAWS triggers an aural alert to notify the flight crew that the aircraft performance is degraded and will be in close proximity to a hazardous condition. In addition, when TAWS detects windshear that improves the aircraft performances, the windshear alerting algorithm triggers an aural alert and provide awareness that degrading performance windshear could be encountered.

To transfer fuel between tanks on the ground with AC power available:
1. Switch on AC fuel pumps of the tank with more fuel.
2. On the Refuel/Defuel Control Panel, open the Defuel Shutoff Valve on the side with more fuel and the Refuel Shutoff Valve on the opposite side.
3. Open the Crossfeed Valve.
4. Upon completion, switch off the AC fuel pumps and close the Refuel Shutoff Valve and the Defuel Shutoff Valve.

During suction defueling, the Defuel Shutoff Valve is opened and the ground defueling equipment provides suction force to the Refuel/Defuel Coupling.

There are two Stall Protection Computers (SPCs). Each SPC can independently initiate stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition. Both SPCs must generate stall pusher commands simultaneously for the stick pusher to activate.

When the aircraft is in flight and close to stall, the Stall Protection System (SPS) engages both stick shakers, providing an aural alert and a warning flag on the PFDs. The stick shakers will continuously jitter as long as the AOA is above their threshold. They deactivate when the AOA decreases by 0.5° below the threshold.
The Stall Protection Computer (SPC) commands AP pitch servo motor to activate the stick pusher. Only when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands at the same time, will the stick pusher activate.

The stick pusher activates only when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands simultaneously.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) provides stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition functions. Specifically, it generates stall alerts through stick shakers and "Stall, Stall, ......" aural warnings. If the Angle of Attack (AOA) continues to increase, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) will automatically command the stick pusher to move the control column forward, preventing an aircraft stall.

The autobrake system is armed when the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to RTO and all Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground, the wheel speed is below 55 kt, and the brake system does not detect a fault. For landing mode, it is armed when the autobrake is set to LO, MED, or HI, the Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate the aircraft is in flight, and the brake system does not detect a fault.

The autobrake is disarmed after arming in any of the following conditions: The brake system detects a fault. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to OFF. An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU). Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals disagree.

When the aircraft is in flight and close to stall, the Stall Protection System (SPS) engages both stick shakers, provides "Stall, Stall, ......" aural alerts, and displays a red warning flag on the PFDs. If the Angle of Attack (AOA) continues to increase, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) automatically commands the pitch servo to move the control column forward to prevent a stall.

Direct tuning is achieved by first pressing the LSK to move the tuning window adjacent to desired location. The RTU concentric tune knobs are then used to set the appropriate frequency/channel in the tuning window. The outer concentric knob is used to adjust the integer digits. The inner concentric knob is used to adjust the decimal digits.

The RTU concentric tune knobs are used to set the appropriate frequency/channel in the tuning window. The outer concentric knob is used to adjust the integer digits, and the inner concentric knob is used to adjust the decimal digits.

The RTU provides integrated control and display of aircraft radio equipment, including selecting the radio frequency (or ATC code) and operating modes of onside radio equipment. The main display page of each radio provides control of all radio frequencies and modes.

The outer concentric knob is used to adjust the integer digits and select SQ0 (or SQ1, SQ2, SQ3), LV (or UV, AM), or any active frequency digit. After the desired field is selected, the inner concentric knob is used to change the value of each digit.

The RTU does not display information for climb, cruise, and descent phases of flight. The RTU top level display page provides tuning control for COM, NAV, ADF, DME, ATC, TCAS, HF, and SELCAL equipment.

The RTU displays frequency for COM, NAV, and ADF radios; hold for DME; transponder code, operating mode, and Flight ID for ATC; operating modes for TCAS; frequency, maritime channel, and emergency channel for HF; and code for SELCAL.
